events.title: The Scillitan Martyrs
events.shortBlurb: Twelve African Christians were beheaded at Carthage in the earliest dated record of the Latin Church…
body: In the reign of Marcus Aurelius, twelve Christians of Scillium in Numidia, seven men and five women, were brought before the proconsul Vigellius Saturninus at Carthage. Their brief trial record, the Acts of the Scillitan Martyrs, is the earliest dated document of the Latin Church and the first to know a Latin Bible.

Offered thirty days in which to reconsider, their spokesman Speratus answered that in so good a cause there was no need of deliberation; and when pressed to swear by the genius of the emperor, he declared, "I recognize not the empire of this world; but rather do I serve that God whom no man hath seen." Saturninus pronounced sentence, and on 17 July 180 the twelve were beheaded.

Their names, Speratus, Nartzalus, Cittinus, Veturius, Felix, Aquilinus, Laetantius, Januaria, Generosa, Vestia, Donata, and Secunda, were kept in honor at Carthage, where a basilica rose over their memory. Tertullian, writing within a generation, numbers Saturninus among the first persecutors of the African church.

events.title: The Carmelites of Compiègne go to the guillotine
events.shortBlurb: Sixteen Carmelite nuns were executed in Paris, singing as they mounted the scaffold…
body: Their deaths came in the Terror's bloodiest weeks. Since the law of 22 Prairial — 10 June 1794 — the revolutionary tribunal of Paris, driven by the prosecutor Fouquier-Tinville, had condemned the accused without witnesses or defense, and the scaffold at the Place du Trône Renversé claimed more than thirteen hundred victims in six weeks.

The Carmelites were convicted on 17 July for living as a religious community and for the royalist letters found in their lodgings; with them died their friend Mulot de la Ménardière. Their bodies went with the day's other dead into the mass graves at Picpus, where their names are now inscribed among the 1,306 buried in the sand-pits there.

French Catholics soon linked their offering to the Terror's sudden end, for Robespierre fell ten days later. The memory of their death outlived the martyrology: it inspired Gertrud von Le Fort's novella The Song at the Scaffold in 1931, a drama by Georges Bernanos, and Francis Poulenc's opera Dialogues of the Carmelites, first staged at La Scala in 1957.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of the Martyrs of Compiègne (vatican.va)
